subject: mathematics
question_text: Using the principle of Mathematical Induction, prove that 3·5⁽²ⁿ⁺¹⁾ + 2⁽³ⁿ⁺¹⁾ is divisible by 17, ∀ n ∈ N.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.21 — LAQ chapter 2, question 11. NOTE: this page prints NO mark split; the 1+1+1+3+1 is the split the same book prints on questions 5, 6, 8 and 10 of this chapter. Publisher's claims until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms them. The book writes the product as 3.5 with a period; it is written here as 3·5 so it cannot be read as three point five. SUPERSEDED 2026-08-31 by the RE-CUT sentence at the end of this note — re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Step 3 — S(k+1) follows. RE-CUT 2026-08-31: this card was filed as LAQ at 8 marks and is now SAQ at 4 marks. The original label came from the Baby Bullet-Q blueprint for the superseded 75-mark paper; the Sri Chaitanya FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition) prints this chapter under a Short Answer Questions banner and prints no long-answer block for it at all. Only the question was taken from a source book; the solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The mathematics and the steps are unchanged; only the mark scheme moved — the four induction moves (base case, hypothesis, inductive step, conclusion) now carry 1 mark each and the opening statement step carries 0. Still unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this by induction — how each power grows, and which subtraction produces the 17.

steps.label: Write the statement
steps.margin_note: Unmarked setup at 4 marks, but never skip it — write divisibility as an equation before anything else.

recall.must_convey: That divisible by 17 is written as the expression equalling 17q for an integer q.
accept: write it as equal to seventeen q where q is an integer
divisible by seventeen means seventeen times some integer
set the whole expression equal to seventeen q
seventeen q ki equal ga rastam

steps.why: Every divisibility induction starts the same way: turn the word into an equation you can substitute.
common_mistakes: Reading 3·5 as the decimal three point five.
steps.memory_tip: Write divisibility as an equation, = 17q with q an integer, before anything else.

steps.label: Check S(1)
steps.margin_note: One mark. The powers are small at n = 1 — work the arithmetic out fully and show the multiple of 17.
lines: which is divisible by 17. So S(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That at n = 1 the value is 3(125) + 16 = 391, and that 391 = 17 × 23.
accept: three times one twenty five plus sixteen is three ninety one which is seventeen times twenty three
at n equals one it comes to three ninety one a multiple of seventeen
five cubed is one twenty five and two to the fourth is sixteen giving three ninety one
n equals one ki three ninety one vasthundi seventeen into twenty three

steps.why: Showing 391 = 17 × 23 rather than just saying 'divisible' is what earns the mark — the examiner wants the multiple named.
common_mistakes: Substituting n = 1 into the exponents wrongly: 2n+1 is 3 and 3n+1 is 4.
Writing 391 and stopping without showing it is 17 × 23.
steps.memory_tip: At n = 1: 3(125) + 16 = 391 = 17 × 23. Work the arithmetic out fully.

steps.label: Assume S(k) is true
steps.margin_note: One mark. Assume for k and number the line — Step 3 substitutes it.
lines: Step 2 — assume S(k) is true, k ∈ N

recall.must_convey: That the statement is assumed for one k, written as 3·5⁽²ᵏ⁺¹⁾ + 2⁽³ᵏ⁺¹⁾ = 17q, and labelled (1).
accept: assume it for k so three times five to the two k plus one plus two to the three k plus one is seventeen q
suppose s of k is true and number it equation one
take the statement as true for some k
k ki true ani assume chesi equation one

steps.why: Both powers grow by a fixed factor when n goes up by one, so the assumption can be used as a whole rather than rearranged.
common_mistakes: Assuming it for every k instead of one k.
steps.memory_tip: Assume for k and NUMBER the line — Step 3 quotes it.

steps.label: Show S(k+1) follows
steps.margin_note: One mark, and the longest step on the page. Each power grows by its own factor: 5² = 25 and 2³ = 8. Substitute for ONE of them and let 17 appear.

recall.must_convey: That going from k to k+1 multiplies the first power by 25 and the second by 8, that (1) is used to replace 3·5⁽²ᵏ⁺¹⁾ by 17q − 2⁽³ᵏ⁺¹⁾, and that 25 − 8 = 17 is what leaves a factor of 17.
accept: the first term picks up twenty five and the second picks up eight then substitute the assumption and twenty five minus eight is seventeen
replace three times five to the two k plus one using equation one and the leftover is seventeen times something
twenty five minus eight equals seventeen which is why it factors
twenty five and eight difference seventeen kabatti factor avuthundi
heard_as: two to the three k plus one

steps.why: 25 − 8 = 17 is the whole reason this works. The question is built backwards from that difference.
common_mistakes: Getting the growth factors wrong: 5⁽²ᵏ⁺³⁾ is 25 × 5⁽²ᵏ⁺¹⁾, not 5 × it.
Substituting for both powers at once, which leaves nothing to cancel.
Not stating that the final bracket is an integer.
steps.memory_tip: Each power grows by its own factor: 5² = 25 and 2³ = 8. Substitute for one of them, and 25 − 8 = 17 appears.

steps.label: Conclude by P.M.I
steps.margin_note: The last mark is for naming the principle. One sentence, one mark.
lines: Hence, by the principle of finite

recall.must_convey: That S(1) is true and S(k) implies S(k+1), so by the principle of mathematical induction the statement holds for every natural number.
accept: since the first case is true and each case gives the next by p m i it is true for all n
hence by the principle of mathematical induction it holds for every natural number
base case plus inductive step gives it for all n in n
p m i prakaram anni n ki true

steps.why: The two proved statements are about n = 1 and about a step. Only the principle turns them into every n.
common_mistakes: Writing 'hence proved' without naming the principle.
steps.memory_tip: The closing sentence names the principle and earns a full mark on its own.
